claim: Masud et al. use attack success probability (ASP) as an attacker-side effectiveness metric
quote: This metric relates to the probability that attacks will be successful.
locator: Sec. 3.5.1 'Attack success probability', p. 9 printed (PDF p. 9)

claim: Masud row, property 1 (campaign persistence): has it in part
quote: Key metrics like attack success probability, attack cost, and attack risk were automatically calculated at intervals using the threat and harm assessment risk model (THARM).
locator: Sec. 3.3, p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7); attack paths 'AP = all_simple_paths (G , Ss, Tr)', Algorithm 2, p. 9
issue: Multi-stage attack paths (behaviour yes), recomputed per interval (qualifier no): partial follows the rule.

claim: Masud row, properties 4 (adaptivity) and 6 (cost-benefit reasoning): has none
quote: Vulnerabilities were prioritized by return on attack, emphasizing those with greatest impact.
locator: Sec. 3.3, p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7); also 'forcing fresh scans and adaptation to new flaws', same paragraph
issue: The paper states RoA prioritisation and attacker adaptation in prose but implements neither in Algorithms 2-3. The dissertation scores this none, while Kim's paper-stated but unimplemented evasion scores 'in part' as 'assumed'. The distinction (Kim's attacker takes the step; Masud's model takes no step) is defensible under Table C.1's caption, but an examiner may see the two as the same kind of authors' assumption.
fix_text: optionally one clause in App. C saying why a paper's prose claim with no modelled step is 'no', not 'assumed'

quote: Tests included widespread and focused attacks aiming to breach many or specific high-value hosts.
issue: Every attack path ends at the database host; nothing chooses among paths, avoids an IDS, keeps MTD patterns or predicts deployments in Algorithms 2-3. 'widespread and focused attacks' are two experimental scenarios, not an attacker's choice.

claim: Masud row in Table 6.1 (copy of Table 3.3 row): 1 in part, rest none
quote: Vulnerabilities were prioritized by return on attack, emphasizing those with greatest impact.
issue: Identical to U0262: marks supported; the none on adaptivity and cost-benefit rests on the 'no modelled step' reading (see U0262).

claim: The paper says its attackers prioritise vulnerabilities by RoA and adapt to new flaws (p. 7)
quote: Vulnerabilities were prioritized by return on attack, emphasizing those with greatest impact. Successful exploitation let adversaries control internals through command channels to connected devices. Watching strategies interact with adversaries showed how movement disrupted plans. IP shuffling and path alteration terminated live links and concealed pathways. Service and operating system diversification modified configurations, forcing fresh scans and adaptation to new flaws.
locator: Sec. 3.3, p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7); pinpoint correct
issue: Both points are on p. 7, but the prioritisation is passive ('Vulnerabilities were prioritized'), with no agent named, and the adaptation is something diversification forces, not something the attackers are said to do. 'its attackers prioritise ... and adapt' assigns an agent the source leaves implicit. Direction is fair.
fix_text: 'says its attackers prioritise vulnerabilities by RoA and adapt to new flaws' -> 'says vulnerabilities were prioritised by RoA and that diversification forced adaptation to new flaws'
